differences.title: 1. LANGUAGE MODEL
differences.leftDesc: Pulumi lets you define infrastructure in real languages (TypeScript, Python, Go, C#), using standard tooling, unit tests, and abstractions. The engine evaluates resources and produces a dependency-aware deployment plan.
differences.rightDesc: CloudFormation uses declarative templates in JSON or YAML. You express resources, parameters, and outputs, while orchestration and dependency resolution are handled by the service. Code reuse is mostly via nested stacks and macros.

differences.title: 2. DIFF & DEPLOY WORKFLOW
differences.leftDesc: Pulumi’s CLI computes resource diffs by comparing desired outputs to stored state, then performs an ordered update that respects dependency graphs. “Preview” simulates changes using the engine’s knowledge of current state.
differences.rightDesc: CloudFormation generates change sets by evaluating the template against the stack’s current state in AWS. It then executes the update in the service’s controlled order, applying resource-level policies and handling replacement semantics.

differences.title: 3. DEPENDENCY & ORDERING
differences.leftDesc: Pulumi builds a dependency graph from actual code references between resource objects. When values flow through outputs, Pulumi infers ordering and parallelism, minimizing race conditions by design rather than requiring explicit DependsOn everywhere.
differences.rightDesc: CloudFormation infers dependencies primarily from intrinsic functions and resource references, plus explicit DependsOn. Execution order is driven by the service while it resolves parameter values and waits for stack-managed resource signals.

differences.title: 4. STATE MANAGEMENT
differences.leftDesc: Pulumi records state per stack in a configurable backend (e.g., Pulumi Service or self-hosted). The engine uses this persisted snapshot to track updates, detect drift, and determine safe operations over time.
differences.rightDesc: CloudFormation maintains stack state within the AWS CloudFormation control plane. Updates and rollback behavior are governed by the stack’s recorded status, events, and resource-level completion data stored server-side.

differences.title: 5. CROSS-CLOUD / PROVIDER ECOSYSTEM
differences.leftDesc: Pulumi can target AWS, Azure, GCP, Kubernetes, and more through provider plugins, while keeping a single programming model. This makes it easier to coordinate multi-cloud resources from one graph and one diff engine.
differences.rightDesc: CloudFormation is tightly coupled to AWS’s provisioning primitives. While there are integrations and external custom resources, the native template lifecycle and resource model are primarily optimized for AWS services and limits.

differences.title: 6. CUSTOM LOGIC EXTENSIBILITY
differences.leftDesc: Pulumi supports arbitrary programmatic logic: loops, conditionals, and strongly typed abstractions that generate resources dynamically. You can compute names, policies, and graph structure before provisioning, then rely on outputs for runtime values.
differences.rightDesc: CloudFormation extends via AWS Lambda-backed custom resources or macros. Templates remain declarative, so custom behavior is implemented outside the template and invoked during stack operations with defined request/response contracts.

differences.title: 7. OPERATIONAL GUARDRAILS
differences.leftDesc: Pulumi integrates policy enforcement using tools like Pulumi Policy Packs and Open Policy Agent workflows. These checks run against planned resource graphs, enabling consistent rules for security, naming, and allowed configurations.
differences.rightDesc: CloudFormation provides stack policies and service-specific mechanisms to constrain updates. Enforcement is largely tied to stack update behavior and AWS managed controls, with less direct visibility into a fully computed desired resource graph.
